sentences.text: Barosaurus lentus is the only known species of the extinct genus Barosaurus, a diplodocid sauropod dinosaur.
It was a large but typical diplodocid with a long neck and a long whip-like tail.
Adult Barosaurus measured between 25 and 27 meters in length and weighed between 12 and 20 metric tons.
Barosaurus had limb bones that were virtually indistinguishable from those of Diplodocus.
Compared to Diplodocus, Barosaurus had a relatively longer neck but a shorter tail.
The head of the Barosaurus skeleton at the American Museum of Natural History reaches the level of the fifth floor.
A 1992 study suggested that Barosaurus would have needed a heart weighing 1.6 tons to pump blood up its very long neck.
There are 19 recorded fossil occurrences of the genus Barosaurus.
A vertebra interpreted as the northernmost record of Barosaurus lentus was described from the Pryor Mountains in Montana, United States, in 2026.
In 2026, researchers reported a Barosaurus specimen with a pathology located in the 'whip' section of its tail.
Barosaurus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1890.
The first Barosaurus remains were discovered in the Morrison Formation of South Dakota by Mrs. E.R. Ellerman and excavated by Othniel Charles Marsh and John Bell Hatcher in 1889.
A Barosaurus specimen was excavated by Earl Douglass at the Carnegie Quarry in the early 20th century and later traded to the Royal Ontario Museum in 1962.
The name Barosaurus comes from the Greek words barys meaning 'heavy' and sauros meaning 'lizard'.
A 2016 preprint by Mike Taylor and Mathew Wedel argued that Barosaurus cervical vertebrae allowed significant lateral neck flexibility but restricted vertical flexibility.

The neck structure suggests Barosaurus had a different feeding style compared to other diplodocids, likely feeding by sweeping its long neck in low arcs along the ground, a strategy first proposed by John Martin in 1987. The restriction in vertical neck flexibility suggests Barosaurus did not primarily feed on vegetation high off the ground.
It is hypothesized that a nuchal ligament may have held Barosaurus' neck in a horizontal position.
Barosaurus may have developed an extremely long neck of about 10 meters to feed over a wide area without moving.
The long neck may also have allowed Barosaurus to radiate excess body heat.
Curator David Evans suggests that sexual selection may have favored individuals with longer necks.
Barosaurus is classified as a member of the sauropod family Diplodocidae and is sometimes placed in the subfamily Diplodocinae with Diplodocus.
Marsh first classified Barosaurus as a diplodocid in 1898, after previously placing it in the family Atlantosauridae in 1896.
Barosaurus lived in present-day North America during the Late Jurassic period, approximately 150 million years ago during the late Kimmeridgian to early Tithonian stages.
Diplodocid fossils, including those of Barosaurus, are found in North America, Europe, and Africa.
It is debated how Barosaurus was depicted in popular media, with Darren Naish noting that late 20th-century books often incorrectly showed it as a short-tailed sauropod with a U-shaped neck.
Paleontologists suspected that Barosaurus africanus was distinct from the North American genus, a view confirmed by a 2006 redescription.
